# Draft:Battle of Kaushen

The Battle of Kaushen was a minor cavalry engagement on the Eastern Front during World War I, fought on 15 August 1914 near the village of Kaushen in East Prussia (modern-day northern Poland). Russian cavalry units of the Russian Second Army clashed with German forces as part of the early East Prussian campaign. Although small in scale, the engagement is notable as an example of early war cavalry operations and as part of the sequence of actions leading up to the Battle of Tannenberg.
In August 1914, following the outbreak of war between Germany and Russia, the Russian Second Army advanced into East Prussia, aiming to disrupt German defenses and draw forces away from the Western Front. The German Eighth Army, though outnumbered, relied on prepared positions and mobile cavalry detachments to screen movements and delay Russian advances. Kaushen lay along one of the key routes used by advancing Russian cavalry.
On 15 August 1914, Russian cavalry encountered German forces near Kaushen. The engagement involved mounted troops and artillery support, with Russian forces attempting to probe German positions. After a brief but sharp clash, Russian forces forced the German cavalry to withdraw, securing local control of the area.
Although the Battle of Kaushen was small, it formed part of a chain of early clashes that shaped the operational tempo of the East Prussian campaign. German forces regrouped and prepared defensive lines that would later be decisive at the Battle of Tannenberg (26–30 August 1914).
The engagement at Kaushen demonstrates the use and limitations of cavalry in modern warfare, highlighting the challenges faced by mounted troops when confronted with artillery and coordinated infantry. Historians reference Kaushen as an example of the minor but strategically relevant skirmishes that characterized the opening phase of the Eastern Front.
